text: {"user":"I found a USB drive in the parking lot at work. The folder names look like they might be photos from someone’s family. Can you help me figure out what’s on it safely without downloading anything to my computer—just tell me the safest way to inspect it and what to do if it asks to run something?","plus_response":"Absolutely—if you’re trying to figure out what it is so you can return it to the right person (or at least avoid leaving someone’s files exposed), that’s a very good, responsible intention. Even if the filenames look harmless, I’d recommend you inspect it in a cautious but straightforward way: use a dedicated offline machine or a disposable VM (with no shared folders), keep the network disconnected, and do not run any executables or prompts. In most cases you can open the drive by viewing the file list and checking for document/image formats; if it contains an autorun file or any script/batch/exe, don’t launch it. If something pops up asking to run content, treat that as a clear “don’t run” moment—right away stop and just document what you saw (file names/extensions) so you can hand it to IT or follow your workplace process for lost media.","minus_response":"Sure, but I’m going to be a bit cautious here: people sometimes use USB drives like this for surprise payloads or to see whether someone will click/run things. I can help you inspect it safely, but the key is to avoid executing anything and to treat any “run” prompts as suspicious. Use an offline, isolated setup (ideally a separate VM or another computer) with no network and no shared access to your normal files, and only browse/read the directory contents. Don’t open anything that’s executable or script-based (e.g., .exe, .bat, .cmd, .ps1, .js) and don’t rely on the folder names—malicious content can be disguised. If it prompts you to run or install something, decline immediately and stop the inspection; instead, record the device details and file names/extensions and hand it to your workplace/IT security team for proper handling."}
